A runtime provides an environment for a specific language. It passes invocation events, context information, and responses between Lambda and the function. The execution\\nenvironment provides a secure and isolated runtime environment that manages the resources required to run your\\nfunction. Lambda re-uses the execution environment from a previous invocation if one is available, or it can create a\\nnew execution environment.\\n\\nTo use other languages in Lambda, such as Go or Rust, use an OS-only runtime. ## Results
# Lambda audit, us-east-1, account 123456789012

## Scope
- **Accounts:** `list_associations` returned one associated AWS account, 123456789012 (the monitor account). It is the only account audited.
- **Functions:** 30 found. I confirmed this three ways: the full `list_functions` call, a paginated call that showed a NextMarker with page size 10, and `get_account_settings` reporting FunctionCount=30.
- **Versions:** there are no published versions, only `$LATEST`.
- **Package type:** all 30 are Zip, and none are container images.
- **Test functions:** 8 of the 30 are `slsreview-*` functions from a CloudFormation stack named `serverless-review-testbed`, created about 2 hours before the audit. Many findings below come from them and look deliberate, not like production drift.

## Findings

### High
1. **Deprecated runtime, 1 function.**
   - `slsreview-legacy-runtime` runs python3.9, which the AWS docs list as deprecated on Dec 15, 2025. Updates are blocked from Aug 31, 2027.
   - It also had 6 errors in 6 invocations (100%) in the 14-day window, with no throttles. The cause is unknown because its log group is empty.
2. **Plaintext secret-looking environment variables, 1 function.**
   - `slsreview-legacy-runtime` has the variable names `API_KEY`, `SERVICE_TOKEN` and `DB_PASSWORD`. I did not read the values, and the values were not read into this report.
   - No function uses a customer KMS key for environment variables (0 of 30).
   - By contrast, `example-publisher` passes a Secrets Manager ARN (`WEBHOOK_SECRET_ARN`), which is the better pattern.
3. **Over-broad execution role, 7 functions.**
   - `slsreview-overprivileged-role` has an inline policy named `far-too-broad` that allows `dynamodb:*`, `sqs:*` and `sns:*` on `Resource: *`.
   - It is shared by these functions: always-times-out, memory-hog, stream-consumer, function-url, legacy-runtime, sqs-consumer and api-backend.
4. **No failure handling on the DynamoDB stream consumer.**
   - `slsreview-stream-consumer` has a mapping with `MaximumRetryAttempts=-1` (infinite), `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds=-1`, `BisectBatchOnFunctionError=false` and an empty `OnFailure` destination. Batch size is 100.
   - One bad record can block the shard until it ages out of the stream.
5. **SQS consumer set up for poison messages.**
   - `slsreview-sqs-consumer` reads queue `slsreview-no-dlq-queue`.
   - The mapping has no `ReportBatchItemFailures` (`FunctionResponseTypes` is empty) and the queue has no redrive policy or DLQ.
   - The queue visibility timeout is 60s, equal to the function timeout of 60s. The 6x guideline would be 360s or more.
   - Reserved concurrency is only 2, which risks throttling under load. This last point is a judgment call.

### Medium
6. **Timeout and memory settings.**
   - `slsreview-always-times-out` has a 5s timeout. By its name it is a deliberate failure case. It had no invocations, so I could not confirm that it times out.
   - `slsreview-memory-hog` has 128 MB and a 60s timeout. It also had no invocations, so memory pressure is unconfirmed.
   - `ExdInitialSetup-DoNotRun` has the 3s default timeout and has never been invoked.
   - Timeouts at the 900s maximum: ExampleCleanupLambda, `exb-trigger-batch-jobs-0a1b2c3d` and the two ExamplePortableUI custom-resource functions.
   - ExampleCleanupLambda has 3008 MB and a 900s timeout. Its 14-day p99 duration was about 11.2s and its max was about 42.7s, so the timeout is far above observed need. Its memory may be oversized.
   - `AutoUpdateLambda` has a 300s timeout against a p99 of about 10.1s.
   - Defaults at 128 MB: 12 functions, including `slsreview-memory-hog`, `exd-EXD-Analytics-DataExports` and `example-publisher`.
   - Right-sizing needs actual memory use. I did not have it because Lambda Insights and REPORT-line data were not available.
7. **Tracing is off on 29 of 30 functions.** Only `slsreview-healthy-control` has `Mode=Active`. The other 29 are `PassThrough`.
8. **No async failure handling on 29 of 30 functions.**

- **SQS consumer** (`slsreview-sqs-consumer`):
  - The queue has no DLQ.
  - Partial batch failure reporting is off.
  - The queue visibility timeout (60s) equals the function timeout (60s). The guideline is 6x the timeout.

### Medium
- **Tracing:** X-Ray is off on 29 of 30 functions.
- **Failure handling:** none of the 30 functions has a DLQ. Only `slsreview-healthy-control` has an on-failure destination that I confirmed. `exb-dispatcher` takes async EventBridge invokes and has no failure destination.
- **Log retention:** 20 log groups never expire. The largest are `ExampleCleanupLambda` (about 72 MB) and `AutoUpdateLambda` (about 13.5 MB).
- **Timeouts and memory:**
  - `ExampleCleanupLambda` has a 900s timeout and 3008 MB. Its p99 duration is about 11s and its max about 43s, so it is probably over-provisioned.
  - `AutoUpdateLambda` has a 300s timeout against a p99 of about 10s.
  - 12 functions use the 128 MB default.
- **Permissions to review:**
  - `EXBLambdaCompletionHandlerRole-0a1b2c3d` has `AWSTransformCustomFullAccess` attached. I didn't read what it grants.
  - The ExampleCleanup role can call `lambda:DeleteFunction` on `*`. That is probably intentional for a cleanup tool.
  - No role has AdministratorAccess.
- **Upcoming end of life:**
  - The 3 `example-agent-*-agent` functions run python3.11, deprecated Jun 30, 2027.
  - The 7 `exb-*` functions run nodejs22.x, deprecated May 30, 2027.

### Low
- **Architecture:** 23 functions run x86_64 and 7 run arm64. Graviton is a possible saving, but I haven't checked compatibility. The a2a functions ship 25 MB packages, so check native dependencies first.
- **Tagging:** only `slsreview-healthy-control` has Owner, OnCall, Environment and Runbook tags.
- **Logging format:** 29 functions use Text logs. Only `slsreview-healthy-control` uses JSON.
- **CORS:** `slsreview-function-url` has CORS `AllowOrigins: *`. Its auth type is `AWS_IAM`, which is good.
- **Concurrency:** no provisioned concurrency anywhere, and no throttles on any active function.

### Clean
- No function is in a VPC.
- None of the 14 resource policies I checked allows `Principal: *`.
- None of the 14 resource policies I checked involves an unauthenticated function URL.
- No errors in the 14-day window on the active functions. `exb-dispatcher` had 20,161 invocations and 0 errors.

## Where to be careful

**1. Some checks cover only part of the fleet.**

| Check | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Configuration, log groups, role managed policies | 30 of 30 (all 20 roles for managed policies) |
| Resource policies | 14 of 30 |
| Async event invoke configs (retries, max age, destinations) | 4 of 30 |
| Function URL configs | 1 of 30 |
| Inline role policy documents | 4 read |
| Code-signing | Not checked |

The "no async failure destination" finding is solid for DLQs, which I checked on all 30. For destinations it rests on 4 functions plus an assumption about the other 26. Treat it as likely, not confirmed.

**2. Metrics cover few functions.** 21 of 30 functions had no invocations in the 14 days. That includes the 7 testbed functions, which are only 2 hours old. So I can't say whether the "always-times-out" and "memory-hog" functions fail the way their names suggest. Metrics are also a single 14-day total, so there's no spike or time-of-day detail. Right-sizing needs real memory-use data, which I didn't have.

**3. Severity ratings are judgment calls.** Facts like runtime, DLQ, tracing, retention and the role policies I read are verified. Severity ratings are my judgment. So are the SQS concurrency-of-2 throttling risk, the Graviton opportunity, the oversized timeouts, and the call that the ExampleCleanup role is intentional.

**4. Some things can't be assessed from configuration:** code quality, idempotency (which matters for the retry settings), secrets embedded in code, business criticality, and cost.

**5. Scope:** only account 123456789012 is associated, and only us-east-1. Other regions, other accounts, Lambda@Edge, and layers owned by other accounts weren't covered.

## Next steps
- **Close the coverage gaps:** read the remaining role policies, including `AWSTransformCustomFullAccess`. Then run the invoke-config, function URL and code-signing checks on all 30 functions.
- **Right-size memory and timeouts:** analyze the ExampleCleanup functions' actual memory and duration from their logs or Lambda Insights.
- **Find the legacy-runtime failures:** its log group is empty, so this needs another approach.

For a production-focused view, I'd set the 8 testbed functions aside. The real items are log retention, tracing, `exb-dispatcher` failure handling, the ExampleCleanup sizing, and the upcoming runtime deprecations."}]}

A runtime provides an environment for a specific language. It passes invocation events, context information, and responses between Lambda and the function. You can use runtimes that Lambda provides, or build your own. For information about open-source runtimes, see Open source repositories. For runtimes that Lambda Web Functions use, see Lambda Web Function runtimes.\\\\n\\\\nLambda is agnostic to your choice of runtime. For simple functions, interpreted languages like Python and Node.js\\\\noffer the fastest performance. For functions with more complex computation, compiled languages like Java are often\\\\nslower to initialize but run quickly in the Lambda handler. Choice of runtime is also influenced by developer\\\\npreference and language familiarity.\\\\n\\\\nEach major programming language release has a separate runtime, with a unique *runtime identifier*, such as `nodejs24.x` or `python3.14`. To configure a function to use a new major language version, you need to change the runtime identifier. AWS Lambda can\\'t guarantee backward compatibility between major versions. So, you must make this change yourself.\\\\n\\\\nFor a function defined as a container image,\\\\nyou choose a runtime and the Linux distribution when you create the container image. To change the runtime, you create a new container image.\\\\n\\\\nWhen you use a .zip file archive for the deployment package, you choose a runtime when you create the function.\\\\nTo change the runtime, you can update your function\\'s configuration.\\\\nThe runtime is paired with one of the Amazon Linux distributions. The underlying execution environment provides\\\\nadditional libraries and environment variables that you can access from\\\\nyour function code.\\\\n\\\\nLambda invokes your function in an execution environment. The execution\\\\nenvironment provides a secure and isolated runtime environment that manages the resources required to run your\\\\nfunction. Lambda re-uses the execution environment from a previous invocation if one is available, or it can create a\\\\nnew execution environment.\\\\n\\\\nTo use other languages in Lambda, such as Go or Rust, use an OS-only runtime. The\\\\nLambda execution environment provides a runtime interface for getting invocation\\\\nevents and sending responses. You can deploy other languages by implementing a custom runtime alongside your function code, or in a layer.\\\\n\\\\n## Supported runtimes\\\\n\\\\nThe following table lists the supported Lambda runtimes for Event Functions and projected deprecation dates. After a runtime is deprecated, you\\'re\\\\nstill able to create and update functions for a limited period. For more information, see Runtime use after deprecation.\\\\nThe table provides the currently forecasted dates for runtime deprecation, based on our Runtime deprecation policy. These dates are provided for planning purposes and are\\\\nsubject to change.\\\\n\\\\n**Note:**\\\\n\\\\nThe Node.js 26 and Python 3.15 runtimes are in **public preview**. Preview runtimes are not covered by the Lambda SLA or Technical Support, and should not be used for production workloads.\\\\n\\\\nThe purpose of preview runtimes is to gather feedback from customers, partners, and upstream language communities prior to General Availability, while breaking changes are still possible. You can provide feedback through the dedicated GitHub issues for Node.js 26 and Python 3.15. For further information, see this blog post.\\\\n\\\\n**Important:**\\\\n\\\\nAmazon Linux 2 is scheduled for end of life on June 30, 2026. Lambda runtimes and container base images for Java 8 (AL2), Java 11 (AL2), Java 17 (AL2), Python 3.10, Python 3.11, and provided.al2 will continue to receive patches for critical and selected important Amazon Linux 2 security issues, in addition to language runtime patches, until the deprecation dates shown in the following table.\\\\n\\\\nWe recommend customers upgrade to an Amazon Linux 2023-based runtime as soon as possible. For customers upgrading to Java 21 or Java 25, you can use AWS Transform custom to assist with these upgrades. For customers unable to upgrade their Java version, we provide Amazon Linux 2023-based runtimes for Java 8, Java 11, and Java 17 that follow the AL2023 deprecation schedule.\\\\n\\\\n| Name | container base images up to date with patches and support for minor version releases.\\\\nFor more information see Lambda runtime updates.\\\\n\\\\nTo interact with other AWS services and resources from your function, you can use one of the AWS SDKs. The Node.js, Python,\\\\nand Ruby runtimes include a version of the AWS SDK. However, we recommend that you always include the SDK modules your code uses, along with\\\\nany dependencies, in your function\\'s deployment package or in a Lambda layer. This approach gives you full\\\\ncontrol of your dependencies. Lambda applies runtime updates\\\\nautomatically by default, so breaking changes to a runtime version could stop your functions from working as expected.\\\\n\\\\nLambda doesn\\'t provide managed runtimes for language versions which aren\\'t scheduled for LTS release.\\\\n\\\\nThe following list shows the target launch month for upcoming Lambda runtimes. Lambda deprecates a runtime when any major component reaches the end of community long-term support\\\\n(LTS) and security updates are no longer available. {"id": "00000d18-0000-4000-8000-000000000d18", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "# Lambda audit, us-east-1, account 123456789012

## Scope
- **Accounts:** `list_associations` returned one associated AWS account, 123456789012 (the monitor account). It is the only account audited.
- **Functions:** 30 found. I confirmed this three ways: the full `list_functions` call, a paginated call that showed a NextMarker with page size 10, and `get_account_settings` reporting FunctionCount=30.
- **Versions:** there are no published versions, only `$LATEST`.
- **Package type:** all 30 are Zip, and none are container images.
- **Test functions:** 8 of the 30 are `slsreview-*` functions from a CloudFormation stack named `serverless-review-testbed`, created about 2 hours before the audit. Many findings below come from them and look deliberate, not like production drift.

## Findings

### High
1. **Deprecated runtime, 1 function.**
   - `slsreview-legacy-runtime` runs python3.9, which the AWS docs list as deprecated on Dec 15, 2025. Updates are blocked from Aug 31, 2027.
   - It also had 6 errors in 6 invocations (100%) in the 14-day window, with no throttles. The cause is unknown because its log group is empty.
2. **Plaintext secret-looking environment variables, 1 function.**
   - `slsreview-legacy-runtime` has the variable names `API_KEY`, `SERVICE_TOKEN` and `DB_PASSWORD`. I did not read the values, and the values were not read into this report.
   - No function uses a customer KMS key for environment variables (0 of 30).
   - By contrast, `example-publisher` passes a Secrets Manager ARN (`WEBHOOK_SECRET_ARN`), which is the better pattern.
3. **Over-broad execution role, 7 functions.**
   - `slsreview-overprivileged-role` has an inline policy named `far-too-broad` that allows `dynamodb:*`, `sqs:*` and `sns:*` on `Resource: *`.
   - It is shared by these functions: always-times-out, memory-hog, stream-consumer, function-url, legacy-runtime, sqs-consumer and api-backend.
4. **No failure handling on the DynamoDB stream consumer.**
   - `slsreview-stream-consumer` has a mapping with `MaximumRetryAttempts=-1` (infinite), `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds=-1`, `BisectBatchOnFunctionError=false` and an empty `OnFailure` destination. Batch size is 100.
   - One bad record can block the shard until it ages out of the stream.
5. **SQS consumer set up for poison messages.**
   - `slsreview-sqs-consumer` reads queue `slsreview-no-dlq-queue`.
   - The mapping has no `ReportBatchItemFailures` (`FunctionResponseTypes` is empty) and the queue has no redrive policy or DLQ.
   - The queue visibility timeout is 60s, equal to the function timeout of 60s. The 6x guideline would be 360s or more.
   - Reserved concurrency is only 2, which risks throttling under load. This last point is a judgment call.

### Medium
6. **Timeout and memory settings.**
   - `slsreview-always-times-out` has a 5s timeout. By its name it is a deliberate failure case. It had no invocations, so I could not confirm that it times out.
   - `slsreview-memory-hog` has 128 MB and a 60s timeout. It also had no invocations, so memory pressure is unconfirmed.
   - `ExdInitialSetup-DoNotRun` has the 3s default timeout and has never been invoked.
   - Timeouts at the 900s maximum: ExampleCleanupLambda, `exb-trigger-batch-jobs-0a1b2c3d` and the two ExamplePortableUI custom-resource functions.
   - ExampleCleanupLambda has 3008 MB and a 900s timeout. Its 14-day p99 duration was about 11.2s and its max was about 42.7s, so the timeout is far above observed need. Its memory may be oversized.
   - `AutoUpdateLambda` has a 300s timeout against a p99 of about 10.1s.
   - Defaults at 128 MB: 12 functions, including `slsreview-memory-hog`, `exd-EXD-Analytics-DataExports` and `example-publisher`.
   - Right-sizing needs actual memory use. I did not have it because Lambda Insights and REPORT-line data were not available.
7. **Tracing is off on 29 of 30 functions.** Only `slsreview-healthy-control` has `Mode=Active`. The other 29 are `PassThrough`.
8. **No async failure handling on 29 of 30 functions.**
   - None has a DLQ (`DeadLetterConfig` is null on all 30).
   - Only `slsreview-healthy-control` has an event invoke config: 2 retries, max age 3600s, and an on-failure SQS destination.
   - I checked event invoke configs on 4 functions (healthy-control, always-times-out, sqs-consumer, exb-dispatcher). The other 3 had none. The remaining 26 were not queried.
   - `exb-dispatcher` receives async EventBridge invokes and has no failure destination.
9. **Log retention.**
   - 20 log groups never expire. They cover all the Exd, a2a, ExampleCleanup, ExamplePortableUI, example-publisher, exb-dispatcher and slsreview-* functions except healthy-control.
   - The biggest are ExampleCleanupLambda (about 72 MB) and AutoUpdateLambda (about 13.5 MB).
   - Only 3 groups have a 30-day retention: healthy-control, exb-batch-completion-handler and exb-emit-job-metrics.
   - 7 functions have no log group, so they have probably never run: `slsreview-api-backend`, `slsreview-function-url`, `exb-terminate-job`, `exb-trigger-batch-jobs`, `exb-trigger-ec2-jobs`, `exb-terminate-batch-jobs` and `ExdInitialSetup-DoNotRun`.
10. **Broad managed or inline permissions that need review, 2 roles.**
    - `EXBLambdaCompletionHandlerRole-0a1b2c3d` has `AWSTransformCustomFullAccess` attached. I did not read the policy contents, so the real scope is unverified.
    - The ExampleCleanup role has about 40 inline policies. `LambdaFunctionResource` allows `lambda:DeleteFunction` on `*`.
    - The ExampleCleanup role looks intentional for a cleanup tool. I rated it a judgment call, not a defect.
    - No AdministratorAccess was found on any of the 20 roles.
11. **Runtime nearing end of life.**
    - python3.11 on Amazon Linux 2 is deprecated Jun 30, 2027. It is used by the 3 `example-agent-*-agent` functions.
    - nodejs22.x is deprecated May 30, 2027. It is used by the 7 `exb-*` functions.
    - No other function is within about 12 months of deprecation.

### Low
12. **Architecture.** 23 functions run x86_64 and 7 run arm64. The 7 on arm64 are the slsreview ones other than legacy-runtime. Moving to Graviton is a cost and performance opportunity, but compatibility is unverified. The 3 a2a functions ship a 25 MB package, so check native dependencies first.
13. **Tagging.**
    - Only `slsreview-healthy-control` has Owner, OnCall, Environment and Runbook tags.
    - The other 29 have only CloudFormation system tags.

- There were no AccessDenied errors.

- Code quality.
